specStatements.text: Students should be able to:
• give examples of the forces involved in stretching, bending or compressing an object
• explain why, to change the shape of an object (by stretching, bending or compressing), more than one force has to be applied – this is limited to stationary objects only
• describe the difference between elastic deformation and inelastic deformation caused by stretching forces.
The extension of an elastic object, such as a spring, is directly proportional to the force applied, provided that the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
force = spring constant × extension
[F = k e]
force, F, in newtons, N
spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m
extension, e, in metres, m
This relationship also applies to the compression of an elastic object, where ‘ e ’ would be the compression of the object.

A force that stretches (or compresses) a spring does work and elastic potential energy is stored in the spring. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done on the spring and the elastic potential energy stored are equal.
Students should be able to:
• describe the difference between a linear and non-linear relationship between force and extension
• calculate a spring constant in linear cases
• interpret data from an investigation of the relationship between force and extension
• calculate work done in stretching (or compressing) a spring (up to the limit of proportionality) using the equation:elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2[E_e = 1/2 k e^2]
Students should be able to calculate relevant values of stored energy and energy transfers.
Required practical activity 6: investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1 and 2.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.

scopeNotes.statement: this is limited to stationary objects only
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every example used to explain why more than one force is needed involves an object that is stationary while it is deformed – a rubber band held at both ends, a spring hanging at rest from a clamp, a diver standing still on a springboard, a compressed suspension spring supporting a parked car. No item asks what happens when a single force acts on a free object that is allowed to accelerate, and no item treats deformation of a moving object. The reasoning offered is always the specification's own: with only one force there would be a resultant force, so a stationary object would not stay stationary.

Every energy calculation using E_e = 1/2 k e² is set below the limit of proportionality, and each stem says so or gives data that stays on the straight part of the graph. Beyond the limit of proportionality the content is qualitative only – students are asked what the curved region shows and how work done then compares with energy stored, never to calculate a value of stored energy there.

concepts.definition: A change in the shape of an object caused by forces acting on it. An object can be deformed by stretching, by bending or by compressing it.
Deformation that makes an object longer. Two forces pull outwards on the object in opposite directions, for example a hand pulling down on a spring while the clamp holding the top pulls up on it.

Deformation that makes an object shorter. Two forces push inwards on the object in opposite directions, for example the weight of a car pushing down on a suspension spring while the wheel assembly pushes up on the bottom of it.

Deformation that curves an object. It needs forces acting in different directions at different places, for example a diver pushing down on the end of a springboard while the support at the fixed end pushes up on it.

concepts.term: Why more than one force is needed
concepts.definition: To change the shape of a stationary object, more than one force has to be applied. A single force would leave a resultant force on the object, so the object would be accelerated instead of deformed. Two or more forces can be arranged so that the resultant is zero and the object stays stationary while its shape changes.
Deformation from which the object returns to its original shape and length once the deforming forces are removed.

Deformation from which the object does not return to its original shape and length once the deforming forces are removed; the change is permanent. The object need not break for the deformation to be inelastic.
The increase in length of a stretched object, that is the stretched length minus the original unstretched length. It is not the total length of the stretched object. Symbol e, measured in metres, m.

The point beyond which the extension of an elastic object is no longer directly proportional to the force applied. The extension of an elastic object, such as a spring, is directly proportional to the force applied provided that the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.

F = k e. This equation must be recalled; it is one of the equations students are required to learn. It links the force applied to an elastic object to the extension it produces, and it holds only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded.
The force needed per metre of extension, symbol k, measured in newtons per metre, N/m. A large spring constant means a stiff spring: a large force produces only a small extension.

concepts.term: Quantities, symbols and units in F = k e
concepts.definition: Force, F, in newtons, N; spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m; extension, e, in metres, m. An extension measured in centimetres or millimetres must be converted to metres before it is used in the equation.

concepts.term: Applying F = k e to compression
concepts.definition: The relationship also applies to the compression of an elastic object, where e would be the compression of the object rather than its extension. Everything else about the equation, its units and its limit of proportionality is unchanged.

concepts.term: Work done and elastic potential energy
concepts.definition: A force that stretches (or compresses) a spring does work and elastic potential energy is stored in the spring. Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done on the spring and the elastic potential energy stored are equal.

concepts.term: Linear relationship between force and extension
concepts.definition: A relationship in which the force–extension graph is a straight line. For a spring below its limit of proportionality the line is straight and passes through the origin, so extension is directly proportional to force and the spring constant is the same for every reading.

concepts.term: Non-linear relationship between force and extension
concepts.definition: A relationship in which the force–extension graph is a curve, so equal increases in force no longer give equal increases in extension. A spring behaves this way once the limit of proportionality has been exceeded, and F = k e can no longer be used.

concepts.term: Finding the spring constant from a graph
concepts.definition: With force on the vertical axis and extension on the horizontal axis, the gradient of the straight part of the line is the spring constant. Reading a large triangle from the line, k = change in force divided by change in extension, with the extension in metres so that k comes out in N/m.

In a table of results, dividing force by extension gives the same value for every reading while the relationship is linear. A reading that breaks the pattern once and then rejoins it is anomalous; readings whose extension per newton keeps growing show that the limit of proportionality has been exceeded.

E_e = 1/2 k e², used to calculate the work done in stretching (or compressing) a spring up to the limit of proportionality. Elastic potential energy, E_e, in joules, J; spring constant, k, in N/m; extension, e, in m. This equation is provided on the equation sheet in the exam, so it does not have to be recalled, but it does have to be selected and used correctly.

Work done on a spring is stored in its elastic potential energy store. When the spring is released it does work on whatever it pushes or pulls, transferring that stored energy – for example to the kinetic energy store of a trolley launched by a compressed spring. If no energy is transferred to the surroundings, the energy transferred equals the elastic potential energy that was stored.

An investigation of the relationship between force and extension for a spring. The spring is hung from a clamp on a clamp stand with a rule fixed vertically beside it, and its unstretched length is measured. Known weights are added one at a time and the new length measured for each load. Extension is found by subtracting the unstretched length from each loaded length, and force is plotted against extension.

concepts.term: AT 1 and AT 2 in this practical
concepts.definition: AT 1 is the use of appropriate apparatus to make and record measurements accurately – here, using a rule to measure the length of the spring. AT 2 is the use of apparatus to measure and observe the effects of forces – here, applying known weights to a spring and observing the extension they produce.

The rule is clamped vertically alongside the spring and the scale is read at eye level, level with the same point on the spring every time, so that parallax error is avoided. The stand is clamped or weighted so it cannot topple, and readings are taken only when the spring has stopped moving.

concepts.term: Working scientifically and maths skills here
concepts.definition: This practical develops working scientifically skills such as identifying anomalous results, repeating readings and drawing a line of best fit rather than joining points, and maths skills such as converting centimetres to metres, calculating the gradient of a linear graph and rearranging F = k e.

misconceptions.question: How many forces must act on a stationary object to change its shape?
misconceptions.correct: More than one force must act on it.
misconceptions.misconception: You only need one force – you just pull the spring and it stretches.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday language you 'pull' a spring with one hand and it stretches, so the second force, exerted by whatever is holding the other end, goes unnoticed.
misconceptions.correction: If only one force acted there would be a resultant force and the stationary object would accelerate away instead of changing shape. The clamp, the hand or the bench at the other end always supplies a second force.

misconceptions.question: Two forces stretch a rubber band. How are they directed?
misconceptions.correct: They act in opposite directions, pulling the two ends apart.
misconceptions.misconception: As long as there are two forces the band stretches, whichever way they point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn the rule 'more than one force' as a counting rule and never check the directions.
misconceptions.correction: Two forces acting the same way would give a resultant force and the object would accelerate. To stretch it, the forces must act in opposite directions so that the resultant is zero and the object is pulled apart.

misconceptions.question: Is a steel spring an elastic object?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It is elastic because it returns to its original shape and length when the forces are removed.
misconceptions.misconception: Elastic means made of rubber or something stretchy, so steel cannot be elastic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday word 'elastic' names a material (an elastic band), so it is read as a description of what something is made of.
misconceptions.correction: In physics, elastic describes the behaviour, not the material. Any object that returns to its original shape and length when the deforming forces are removed has been elastically deformed, including steel springs.

misconceptions.question: A wire is stretched and stays permanently longer. Has it been inelastically deformed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It did not return to its original length, so the deformation was inelastic.
misconceptions.misconception: Inelastic deformation means the object snaps or breaks apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Inelastic' sounds like total failure, and demonstrations of overstretched springs often end with something breaking.
misconceptions.correction: Inelastic deformation only means the object does not return to its original shape and length. A permanently stretched spring that is still in one piece has been inelastically deformed.

misconceptions.question: A spring is 4.0 cm long unstretched and 6.5 cm long with a load on it. What is the extension?
misconceptions.correct: 2.5 cm, the loaded length minus the unstretched length.
misconceptions.misconception: The extension is 6.5 cm, because that is how long the stretched spring is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ruler reading next to the bottom of the loaded spring is the number in front of the student, so it gets recorded as 'the extension'.
misconceptions.correction: Extension is the increase in length, so the original length must be subtracted every time. Using total length instead makes the force–extension graph miss the origin and gives the wrong spring constant.

misconceptions.question: Is extension always directly proportional to the force applied to a spring?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is directly proportional only provided that the limit of proportionality is not exceeded.
misconceptions.misconception: F = k e works for any force, because it is the equation for springs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every worked example and every graph students meet first is linear, so the condition attached to the rule is treated as small print.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states the proportionality only holds provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded. Past that point the graph curves and F = k e cannot be used.

misconceptions.question: What happens at the limit of proportionality?
misconceptions.correct: Extension stops being directly proportional to force, so the graph stops being a straight line.
misconceptions.misconception: The limit of proportionality is the force at which the spring snaps.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'limit' suggests a breaking point, and it is the last thing marked on the graphs students see.
misconceptions.correction: The spring is still intact and still stretching past that point; what changes is that equal increases in force no longer give equal increases in extension.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of the spring constant?
misconceptions.correct: Newtons per metre, N/m.
misconceptions.misconception: The spring constant is a force, so it is measured in newtons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol k appears in F = k e alongside F, and 'constant' does not suggest a unit of its own.
misconceptions.correction: The spring constant is force per unit extension, so its unit is newtons per metre, N/m. It tells you how many newtons are needed for each metre of extension.

misconceptions.question: Spring A has k = 20 N/m and spring B has k = 60 N/m. Which stretches more for the same force?
misconceptions.correct: Spring A, because it has the smaller spring constant.
misconceptions.misconception: Spring B stretches more, because a bigger spring constant means more stretch.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Bigger number means more' is a strong default, and k is rarely described in words as force per metre.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging F = k e gives e = F / k, so for a fixed force the extension is smaller when k is larger. A large spring constant means a stiff spring.

misconceptions.question: How is the spring constant found from a force–extension graph?
misconceptions.correct: It is the gradient of the line when force is on the vertical axis and extension is on the horizontal axis.
misconceptions.misconception: The gradient is the spring constant whichever way round the axes are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'gradient = spring constant' as a slogan without tying it to which quantity is on which axis.
misconceptions.correction: Gradient is always the vertical quantity divided by the horizontal one. With extension plotted on the vertical axis the gradient is e / F, which is 1 / k, so it must be inverted to give the spring constant.

misconceptions.question: The extension of a spring is doubled below the limit of proportionality. What happens to the energy stored?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes four times as large, because energy depends on the square of the extension.
misconceptions.misconception: Doubling the extension doubles the energy stored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force and extension are proportional, so students carry that linear thinking straight over to the energy.
misconceptions.correction: In E_e = 1/2 k e² the extension is squared, so doubling e multiplies the stored energy by 2² = 4. Both the force and the distance moved double, which is why the energy rises by a factor of four.

misconceptions.question: A spring extends by 12 cm under a 6.0 N force. What is the spring constant?
misconceptions.correct: 50 N/m, using an extension of 0.12 m.
misconceptions.misconception: 6.0 divided by 12 gives 0.50 N/m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number on the ruler is in centimetres, and the equation looks the same whatever units are used, so the conversion is skipped.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives extension, e, in metres, m. Converting 12 cm to 0.12 m before dividing gives k = 6.0 / 0.12 = 50 N/m.

misconceptions.question: Does F = k e apply to a spring that is being squashed?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The relationship also applies to compression, where e is the compression of the object.
misconceptions.misconception: F = k e is the stretching equation, so a different rule is needed for compression.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every example and every graph in class is a stretching one, and the symbol is introduced as 'extension'.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that the relationship also applies to the compression of an elastic object, with e standing for the compression instead of the extension.

misconceptions.question: A spring is stretched without being inelastically deformed. Is all the work done stored as elastic potential energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The work done on the spring and the elastic potential energy stored are equal.
misconceptions.misconception: Some energy is always wasted, so the spring must store less than the work done.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Some energy is always dissipated' is a rule students meet for machines and carry across to every energy question.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is precise: provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, the work done on the spring and the elastic potential energy stored are equal.

misconceptions.question: A force–extension graph curves after the last few readings. Are those readings wrong?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. A curve is what a spring shows once the limit of proportionality has been exceeded.
misconceptions.misconception: The graph should be a straight line, so any point off the line is an anomaly to be ignored.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are taught to look for anomalies and to expect straight lines, so a curve looks like bad measurement.
misconceptions.correction: An anomaly is a single point off the pattern that the next readings return to. A run of readings that curve steadily away shows real non-linear behaviour past the limit of proportionality.

misconceptions.question: Beyond the limit of proportionality each extra newton produces a bigger extension. Has the spring become stiffer?
misconceptions.correct: No. It has become less stiff, because more extension is produced per newton.
misconceptions.misconception: The graph bends, so the spring must be getting stiffer as the load grows.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any change in a graph past a marked point is read as 'the spring is now harder to stretch', and the direction of the bend is not checked.
misconceptions.correction: With force on the vertical axis, the gradient falls in the curved region. A smaller gradient means a smaller force per metre of extension, so the spring is easier, not harder, to stretch.

misconceptions.question: What does the area under a force–extension graph represent?
misconceptions.correct: The work done on the spring, which equals the elastic potential energy stored in it.
misconceptions.misconception: The area under the line gives the spring constant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Gradient and area are both 'things you get off a graph', and students who are unsure which is which pick either one.
misconceptions.correction: The gradient of a force–extension line gives the spring constant; the area beneath it gives the energy stored. They answer different questions and have different units.

misconceptions.question: A spring hangs from a clamp with a mass on the bottom. How many forces stretch it?
misconceptions.correct: Two: the downward pull of the mass and the upward pull of the clamp.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the weight acts on the spring, so one force is stretching it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The mass is what the student added, so it is the only force they notice; the clamp is seen as a piece of apparatus rather than a source of force.
misconceptions.correction: The clamp pulls up on the top of the spring with an equal force. Without it the whole arrangement would simply fall, and the spring would not be stretched at all.

misconceptions.question: A spring with k = 200 N/m is stretched by 0.20 m. How much energy is stored?
misconceptions.correct: 4.0 J, from E_e = 1/2 k e².
misconceptions.misconception: The force is 40 N and the extension is 0.20 m, so the energy is 40 × 0.20 = 8.0 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work done = force × distance is a familiar equation, and students apply it with the final force rather than using the elastic energy equation.
misconceptions.correction: The force grows from zero to its final value as the spring stretches, which is where the factor of 1/2 comes from. The equation to use is E_e = 1/2 k e², giving 0.5 × 200 × 0.20² = 4.0 J.

misconceptions.question: A spring is stretched so far that it is permanently deformed. Does the work done still equal the energy stored?
misconceptions.correct: No. Once the spring is inelastically deformed the two are no longer equal.
misconceptions.misconception: Work done always equals the elastic potential energy stored, whatever happens to the spring.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equality is memorised as a fact and the condition attached to it in the specification is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: The specification attaches a condition: the two are equal provided the spring is not inelastically deformed. Once it is, some of the work done has gone into permanently changing the spring, so the energy stored elastically is less than the work done.

misconceptions.question: Does a compressed spring store elastic potential energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Work is done in compressing it and elastic potential energy is stored.
misconceptions.misconception: Energy is only stored when a spring is stretched, because storing energy means pulling something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy stores are introduced with stretched bands and catapults, so compression is never pictured as a way of storing energy.
misconceptions.correction: A force that stretches or compresses a spring does work either way, and elastic potential energy is stored either way. A compressed spring in a toy or a car suspension releases that stored energy when it expands.

misconceptions.question: A spring is stretched past the point of permanent deformation. Was work done on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A force moved the end of the spring, so work was done on it.
misconceptions.misconception: The spring does not spring back, so no work can have been done on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work is confused with the energy that is usefully recovered, so if nothing comes back students conclude nothing went in.
misconceptions.correction: Work is done whenever a force moves its point of application. The work done is greater than the elastic potential energy stored, because part of it went into deforming the spring permanently.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter where your eye is when reading the rule beside a hanging spring?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The scale must be read at eye level, level with the point being measured.
misconceptions.misconception: A ruler reading is a ruler reading, so eye position cannot change it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rulers are used from primary school onwards without anyone mentioning parallax, so the idea that the reading depends on viewing angle is new.
misconceptions.correction: Looking from above or below the mark makes the pointer appear against the wrong part of the scale. This parallax error can be several millimetres, which is large compared with the extensions being measured.

misconceptions.question: How should the length of the loaded spring be measured?
misconceptions.correct: In place, hanging vertically, with the rule fixed vertically beside it.
misconceptions.misconception: Take the spring off the stand and lay it flat on the bench to measure it properly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Measuring something flat on a bench feels easier and more accurate than measuring it hanging in mid-air.
misconceptions.correction: Removing the load removes the stretching force, so the spring returns to its unstretched length if the deformation was elastic. The loaded length must be measured while the load is still hanging.

misconceptions.question: Two springs are pulled by the same force. Does the stiffer one store more energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. For the same force, the stiffer spring stores less elastic potential energy.
misconceptions.misconception: A stiffer spring is harder to stretch, so it must store more energy for the same force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Stiff' feels like 'strong', and effort is confused with energy without checking how far the end actually moves.
misconceptions.correction: For the same force the stiffer spring extends less, and energy stored depends on the extension as well as the force. With three times the spring constant the extension is one third, and the energy stored is one third as large.

mcqs.stem: A student holds a rubber band at both ends and pulls so that it stretches. Which statement about the forces on the band is correct?

options.text: Two forces act on the band, pulling its ends in opposite directions.
options.rationale: Deforming a stationary object needs more than one force, and to stretch it they must pull the ends apart.

options.text: One force acts on the band, pulling it along its own length.
options.rationale: Students count only the pull they are consciously applying and forget the second hand.

options.text: Two forces act on the band, pulling both ends the same way.
options.rationale: The 'more than one force' rule is remembered as a count without checking directions.

options.text: The only force acting on the band is its own weight, which stretches it.
options.rationale: Weight is the force students name first for any hanging or held object.

mcqs.stem: Why must more than one force act on a stationary object in order to change its shape?

options.text: One force on its own is always too weak to change the shape of an object.
options.rationale: Deformation is treated as a matter of strength rather than of resultant force.

options.text: Two forces are needed so that twice as much energy is stored in the object.
options.rationale: Energy ideas are imported into a question that is about forces and motion.

options.text: One force alone gives a resultant force, so the object would move instead of deform.
options.rationale: A single force leaves a non-zero resultant, which accelerates the object rather than deforming it.

options.text: One force must stretch the object while the other one compresses it.
options.rationale: 'Opposite directions' is misread as one force stretching and one squashing.

mcqs.stem: A diver stands still on the end of a springboard and the board bends. Which pair of forces is bending the board?

options.text: Only the downward push of the diver acts, so only one force bends it.
options.rationale: The support is seen as apparatus rather than as a source of force.

options.text: The downward push of the diver and the upward force from the board's support.
options.rationale: Bending needs forces acting in different directions at different places on the board.

options.text: The diver's weight and the diver's mass act together on the board.
options.rationale: Mass is treated as a second force rather than as a property of the diver.

options.text: The upward push of the board on the diver and the diver's weight.
options.rationale: Any two forces are accepted, without checking that both act on the board.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes elastic deformation?

options.text: The object is made of rubber or another material that feels stretchy.
options.rationale: The everyday meaning of 'elastic' as a material is used instead of the physics meaning.

options.text: The object stretches so far that it breaks into two separate pieces.
options.rationale: Elastic and inelastic are read as degrees of damage rather than as behaviours.

options.text: The object keeps its new shape and its new length once the forces are taken away.
options.rationale: This describes inelastic deformation, so the two definitions have been swapped.

options.text: The object returns to its original shape and length when the forces are removed.
options.rationale: This is the defining difference between elastic and inelastic deformation.

mcqs.stem: A steel spring is stretched by a large force. When the force is removed the spring is longer than it was at the start. What has happened to the spring?

options.text: It has been inelastically deformed and will not return to its original length.
options.rationale: Failure to return to the original length after the forces are removed is inelastic deformation.

options.text: It has been elastically deformed, because steel springs are always elastic.
options.rationale: Elastic is treated as a fixed property of the material rather than of the behaviour.

options.text: It has been elastically deformed, because it did not break or snap apart.
options.rationale: Inelastic deformation is assumed to require breakage.

options.text: It has not been deformed at all, since the force that stretched it is no longer acting.
options.rationale: Deformation is thought to exist only while the force is applied.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched by a 4 N force and is 3 cm longer while the force acts. When the force is removed it returns to its starting length. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The deformation was inelastic, because the spring changed length while loaded.
options.rationale: Any change of length at all is taken to mean inelastic deformation.

options.text: The deformation was inelastic, because energy was needed to stretch the spring.
options.rationale: Doing work on the spring is confused with damaging it permanently.

options.text: The deformation was elastic, because the spring returned to its original length.
options.rationale: The test is what happens after the forces are removed, and the spring recovered fully.

options.text: No deformation happened, because the spring ended up the same length as before.
options.rationale: Deformation is judged only from the final state, ignoring what happened under load.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the extension of a spring is correct?

options.text: Extension is directly proportional to force for any force that is applied.
options.rationale: The condition attached to the proportionality is dropped as small print.

options.text: Extension is directly proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality.
options.rationale: This is the relationship exactly as the specification states it, condition included.

options.text: Extension is directly proportional to the total length of the loaded spring.
options.rationale: Extension is confused with the total length read off the rule.

options.text: Extension is directly proportional to the square of the force applied to it.
options.rationale: The square in the energy equation is carried over into the force equation.

mcqs.stem: Force is plotted on the vertical axis and extension on the horizontal axis for a spring. Below the limit of proportionality, what does the graph look like?

options.text: A straight line with a positive intercept.
options.rationale: Plotting total length instead of extension shifts the line off the origin.

options.text: A curve that gets steeper as force increases.
options.rationale: Any spring graph is assumed to curve at some point.

options.text: A curve that levels off as force increases.
options.rationale: The shape of graphs that reach a maximum is applied here by habit.

options.text: A straight line that passes through the origin.
options.rationale: Directly proportional quantities give a straight line through the origin.

mcqs.stem: A force–extension graph for a spring is a straight line up to 8 N, then curves so that each extra newton produces a larger extension. What does the curved part show?

options.text: The limit of proportionality has been exceeded.
options.rationale: Past that limit, equal increases in force no longer give equal increases in extension.

options.text: The spring must have snapped at a force of 8 N.
options.rationale: 'Limit' is read as a breaking point.

options.text: The results above 8 N are anomalous and wrong.
options.rationale: A departure from a straight line is assumed to be measurement error.

options.text: The spring has become stiffer above 8 N.
options.rationale: The bend in the line is read as increased stiffness without checking the gradient.

mcqs.stem: What is the unit of the spring constant, k?

options.text: newtons per kilogram, N/kg
options.rationale: The unit of gravitational field strength is recalled instead.

options.text: newtons times metres, N m
options.rationale: The multiplication in F = k e is applied to the units the wrong way round.

options.text: newtons per metre, N/m
options.rationale: The spring constant is the force needed per metre of extension.

options.text: metres per newton, m/N
options.rationale: This is extension per newton, the gradient of the graph with the axes swapped.

mcqs.stem: A spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m. It is stretched so that its extension is 0.08 m. Calculate the force applied to the spring.

options.rationale: The extension is used as 8 cm instead of 0.08 m.
The spring constant is divided by the extension instead of multiplied.
The extension is divided by the spring constant.

options.text: 2 N

mcqs.stem: A force of 6.0 N stretches a spring by 12 cm. The limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. Calculate the spring constant.

options.rationale: The extension is left in centimetres.

options.text: 50 N/m

options.rationale: Extension is divided by force, and left in centimetres: 12 / 6.0.

options.text: 72 N/m
options.rationale: Force and extension are multiplied rather than divided.

mcqs.stem: Force is plotted against extension for a spring and the result is a straight line. How is the spring constant found from this graph?

options.text: It is the gradient of the straight part of the line.
options.rationale: With force on the vertical axis, gradient is force divided by extension, which is k.

options.text: It is the gradient of extension plotted against force.
options.rationale: The gradient rule is remembered without tying it to the axes.

options.text: It is the area under the straight part of the line.
options.rationale: Area and gradient are confused; the area gives the energy stored.

options.text: It is the point where the line crosses the force axis.
options.rationale: An intercept is picked because it is another value read off a graph.

mcqs.stem: A spring is 5.0 cm long. When a force of 7.0 N is applied it becomes 8.5 cm long. Calculate the spring constant of the spring.

options.text: 82 N/m
options.rationale: The loaded length of 0.085 m is used instead of the extension.
The extension in centimetres is divided by the force.
The force is multiplied by the extension in centimetres.

mcqs.stem: A spring is squashed rather than stretched. Which statement is correct?

options.text: F = k e does not apply, because springs only stretch elastically.
options.rationale: The equation is tied to the word 'extension' and not generalised.

options.text: No energy is stored, because energy is only stored by stretching.
options.rationale: Energy storage is pictured only as pulling something out of shape.

options.text: F = k e applies, but the spring constant is negative for a squash.
options.rationale: A sign is invented to represent the change of direction.

options.text: F = k e still applies, with e as the compression of the spring.
options.rationale: The specification states the relationship also applies to compression, with e as the compression.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched and is not inelastically deformed. What is true about the work done on the spring?

options.text: It is greater than the elastic potential energy stored there.
options.rationale: Students assume energy is always partly wasted.

options.text: It is equal to the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.
options.rationale: Provided the spring is not inelastically deformed, work done and energy stored are equal.

options.text: It is double the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.
options.rationale: The factor of 1/2 in the energy equation is read as energy lost.

options.text: It is smaller than the elastic potential energy stored there.
options.rationale: The relationship is reversed, treating the spring as an energy source.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched so far that it is inelastically deformed. How does the work done on it compare with the elastic potential energy stored?

options.text: The work done is greater than the elastic potential energy stored.
options.rationale: The two are equal only if the spring is not inelastically deformed; part of the work has permanently deformed it.

options.text: The work done is exactly equal to the elastic potential energy stored.
options.rationale: The equality is remembered without the condition attached to it.

options.text: The work done is smaller than the elastic potential energy stored.
options.rationale: The inequality is applied in the wrong direction.

options.text: No work is done once the spring is inelastically deformed.
options.rationale: Work is confused with the energy that can be recovered.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 200 N/m is stretched by 0.20 m, which is below its limit of proportionality. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.

options.rationale: The extension is not squared, so energy is treated as proportional to extension.
The factor of 1/2 is left out, giving force × extension = 40 × 0.20.
k e is calculated, which is the force in newtons, and quoted as the energy.

mcqs.stem: The extension of a spring is doubled, staying below the limit of proportionality. What happens to the elastic potential energy stored in it?

options.text: It becomes two times as large.
options.rationale: The linear force–extension relationship is applied to the energy.

options.text: It becomes four times as large.
options.rationale: E_e depends on e², so doubling the extension multiplies the energy by 2² = 4.

options.text: It becomes eight times as large.
options.rationale: The doubling is applied to the force, the extension and the equation itself.

options.text: It stays the same as before.
options.rationale: Stored energy is assumed to depend only on the spring constant.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 800 N/m is compressed by 3.0 cm and then released, pushing a trolley. If no energy is transferred to the surroundings, how much energy is transferred to the kinetic energy store of the trolley?

options.rationale: The compression is not squared, so energy is treated as proportional to it.
The factor of 1/2 is left out, giving force × compression.
The compression is used as 3.0 m instead of 0.030 m.
E_e = 0.5 × 800 × 0.030² = 0.36 J, and all of it is transferred to the trolley.

mcqs.stem: In the required practical on force and extension, how is the extension found for each load?

options.text: By subtracting the unstretched length from the loaded length.
options.rationale: Extension is the increase in length, so the original length must be subtracted.

options.text: By reading the total length of the spring from the rule.
options.rationale: The number read off the rule is recorded as the extension.

options.text: By adding the unstretched length to the loaded length each time.
options.rationale: The operation is remembered as combining two lengths.

options.text: By measuring the spring again after the load has been removed.
options.rationale: The loaded length is thought to be recoverable once the load is off.

mcqs.stem: Which technique gives the most accurate measurement of the length of the loaded spring?

options.text: Hold the rule at an angle so the whole spring is in view.
options.rationale: Seeing the apparatus clearly is confused with measuring it accurately.

options.text: Hold the rule vertical and read the scale at eye level.
options.rationale: A vertical rule read at eye level avoids parallax error.

options.text: Read the scale from above so the top of the spring shows.
options.rationale: Viewing angle is assumed not to affect a ruler reading.

options.text: Take the spring off and measure it flat on the bench.
options.rationale: Measuring on a bench feels easier than measuring in mid-air.

mcqs.stem: A student measures the extension of a spring: 1.0 N, 2.0 cm; 2.0 N, 4.0 cm; 3.0 N, 6.0 cm; 4.0 N, 8.0 cm; 5.0 N, 11.5 cm; 6.0 N, 16.0 cm. What do the last two readings show?

options.text: The last two readings are anomalies caused by a mistake.
options.rationale: Any departure from a straight line is assumed to be experimental error.

options.text: The spring must have snapped under the 5.0 N load.
options.rationale: The limit of proportionality is read as a breaking point.

options.text: The limit of proportionality has been passed after 4.0 N.
options.rationale: Extension per newton keeps growing after 4.0 N, so the relationship is no longer linear.

options.text: The spring constant of the spring has increased.
options.rationale: A larger extension per newton is misread as a larger spring constant.

mcqs.stem: A force–extension graph for a spring is a straight line through the origin passing through the point extension = 0.15 m, force = 30 N. Calculate the spring constant.

options.rationale: Force and extension are multiplied instead of divided.
Extension is divided by force, giving 1 / k.
The extension is used as 15 cm instead of 0.15 m.
k is the gradient, 30 / 0.15 = 200 N/m.

mcqs.stem: Spring A has a spring constant of 30 N/m and spring B has a spring constant of 90 N/m. The same force is applied to each spring. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Spring B extends three times as much as spring A.
options.rationale: A bigger spring constant is read as more stretch.

options.text: Spring B extends one third as much as spring A does.
options.rationale: e = F / k, so tripling the spring constant divides the extension by three.

options.text: Spring B and spring A extend by exactly the same amount.
options.rationale: The same force is assumed to give the same extension in any spring.

options.text: Spring B stores three times as much energy as spring A.
options.rationale: Stiffness is equated with energy stored, ignoring the smaller extension.
